samples.text:
Some governments are now testing a system where every adult get a regular amount of money, even if they do not have a job. In my opinion, this is a positive development, although there are some problems with the idea.

The most important advantage is that a basic income can reduce poverty. Many people today have jobs that pay very little or are not stable, so they worry about paying for rent and food. If everyone receive a fixed amount every month, nobody will be extremely poor. This can also reduce stress and make people more healthy and happy.

Another advantage is that basic income give people more freedom. For example, a person who wants to study a new skill or start a small business can do it without being afraid of losing all their money. Also, people who take care of their children or old parents at home can receive some money for their important work, which is usually unpaid.

On the other hand, many people think that basic income is too expensive for the government, and it may need to raise taxes. Some people also believe that if people get free money, they will become lazy and stop working. However, I think most people want to work because they want a better life, not only to survive.

In conclusion, I believe that experimenting with basic income is a positive development, because it can reduce poverty and give people more choices in their life. Of course, governments must test it carefully first to see if they can afford it.
samples.why: Clear positive position · relevant ideas and counter-arguments but limited development · mechanical linking · adequate vocabulary · recurring subject-verb agreement errors and a comparative error that do not obscure meaning.

samples.text:
In several countries, governments have begun trials in which every adult receives a fixed sum of money at regular intervals, regardless of whether they are employed. Although the aim of reducing poverty is admirable, I believe that this is essentially a negative development.

Supporters argue that a basic income would provide security in an economy where many jobs are low-paid, temporary or at risk from automation. It would also be simpler to administer than complex welfare systems, and it would recognise unpaid work such as caring for children or elderly relatives.

However, the most serious problem is cost. Giving a meaningful amount of money to every adult, including those who are already wealthy, would require an enormous budget. To fund it, governments would probably have to raise taxes significantly or cut spending on other public services, such as healthcare and education, which the poorest people depend on most. In this sense, a universal payment may be a less efficient way of helping those in need than targeted support.

Another concern is the possible effect on work. While most people would continue working, some might reduce their hours or leave jobs that are unpleasant but necessary, such as cleaning or care work. If this happened on a large scale, it could cause labour shortages and slow economic growth, which in turn would make the scheme even harder to afford. Moreover, there is a risk that the payments push up prices, particularly rents, so that people is no better off in real terms.

In conclusion, although a basic income aims to give everyone financial security, its high cost and potential impact on employment and prices make it an unwise policy. I therefore regard governments' experiments with it as a negative development, and believe that resources would be better spent on improving existing welfare systems.
samples.why: Clear negative position throughout · opposing arguments summarised then own ideas well extended · logical progression · good vocabulary (targeted support, labour shortages) · mostly error-free with an occasional agreement slip.

samples.text:
A number of governments have launched trials in which adults receive a regular, unconditional payment, irrespective of whether they are in work. Whether a universal basic income would succeed as a permanent national policy remains highly uncertain, but I believe that the decision to test it is a clearly positive development.

The case for exploring the idea is compelling. Many welfare systems are complex, stigmatising and riddled with gaps, leaving people who are entitled to support unable to obtain it. Meanwhile, insecure employment and the prospect of automation have left many workers exposed to sudden losses of income. An unconditional payment could provide a stable foundation, allowing people to retrain, care for relatives or take the risk of starting a business without fear of destitution.

Equally, the objections to basic income are serious and deserve to be tested rather than assumed. Critics warn that it would be ruinously expensive, that it might discourage people from working and that landlords and retailers could simply absorb the extra money through higher prices. These are empirical questions, and debates about them have long been conducted largely on the basis of ideology. Carefully designed experiments can reveal how recipients actually behave, how much the policy would really cost and which groups benefit most.

It should be acknowledged that trials have limitations. Because they are small and temporary, participants may behave differently than they would under a permanent scheme, and a pilot in one region cannot fully reflect the economic effects of a national programme. Nevertheless, imperfect evidence is preferable to none, and gradual experimentation is far less risky than either adopting such a radical policy wholesale or rejecting it without investigation.

In conclusion, whatever the eventual verdict on basic income itself, governments that test it are approaching a difficult question in a responsible, evidence-based way. For that reason, I regard these experiments as a positive development.
samples.why: Clear, precisely framed positive judgement · distinguishes the policy from experimenting with it · ideas fully extended and evaluated · cohesion managed skilfully · wide, precise vocabulary (destitution, empirical) · error-free, sophisticated structures.
